title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right level of politeness, give your name, ask how someone is, and see from the very first line that Slovak has no articles at all.
bekal: greet people with *ahoj*, *dobrý deň*, and *dobré ráno*, each in its proper place
give your name with *volám sa…* and ask someone else's name at two levels of politeness
use all six forms of *byť* and negate them with *nie som* — the only verb whose negative takes two words

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Prvý deň v jazykovej škole
dialogs.intro: The first day of a language course at a language school in Bratislava. Two new students sit side by side.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ahoj! Volám sa Budi. A ty?
lines.id: Hi! My name is Budi. And you?
lines.literal: hi! I-call self Budi. and you?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: I'm Eva. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Ďakujem, mám sa dobre. A ty?
lines.literal: I-thank, I-have self well. and you?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Áno, som Slovenka. Ty si Číňan?
lines.id: Yes, I'm Slovak. Are you Chinese?
lines.literal: yes, I-am Slovak-woman. you you-are Chinese-man?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nie, nie som Číňan. Som Indonézan.
lines.id: No, I'm not Chinese. I'm Indonesian.
lines.literal: no, not I-am Chinese-man. I-am Indonesian-man.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: To je zaujímavé! Vitaj na Slovensku!
lines.id: Oh, how interesting! Welcome to Slovakia!
lines.literal: that is interesting! be-welcome in Slovakia!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ďakujem pekne! Zajtra sa uvidíme, Eva.
lines.id: Thank you very much! See you tomorrow, Eva.
lines.literal: I-thank nicely! tomorrow self we-will-see, Eva.

notes: **Ahoj works both ways.** One word for "hi" and "bye" — just like Italian *ciao*. It's casual: for friends, fellow students, and people your age. With people you don't know, use *dobrý deň*.

**Ako sa voláš? is not "what is your name".** Literally it's "how do you call yourself" — you're asking how the person **calls themselves**. So the answer mirrors it: *volám sa Budi* = "I call myself Budi". The little word *sa* is that mirror, and it will appear with dozens of other verbs throughout this course.

**Teší ma literally means "it pleases me".** The subject is the introduction itself, not you. The full form is *teší ma, že vás spoznávam*, but the two words are enough and you'll actually hear them more often.

**No articles. None at all.** Look at *Som Slovenka* — no *a* or *the* in front, and not a single one in this whole dialogue. *Kniha* means "book", "a book", and "the book" all at once, and you never have to choose. Context does the work English gives to *a* and *the*; after a week you'll stop missing them.

**Áno and nie.** *Áno* = yes (the casual form *hej* is very common among young people). *Nie* = no/not. Notice that *nie* appears twice in Budi's line with different jobs: the first answers the question, the second negates the verb.

grammars.title: Byť — the only verb whose negative takes two words
body: The first verb you must master, and also the most irregular. Learn these two columns together from the start — separating them only makes it harder.
after: **The pronoun can be dropped.** The verb ending already carries the subject, so *Som Slovenka* can only mean "I'm Slovak". *Ja* is used only when you want **emphasis**: *Ja som Eva* = "Me, I'm Eva". In the dialogue above Eva uses it for exactly that — she's taking her turn.

**All other verbs negate with a joined prefix *ne-***: *nemám* (I don't have), *nerozumiem* (I don't understand), *nechcem* (I don't want). Only *byť* uses the separate word *nie*. If you hear yourself say *nesom*, that is the one place the general rule doesn't apply.

**The word *som* is never stressed.** It clings to the word before it like a tail, so *volám sa* sounds like one word: **VOH**-lahm-sah. This holds for the whole family of short words — *som, si, je, sme, ste, sú, sa, si, ma, ťa* — and explains why Slovak sounds flowing even though its stress is stuck at the front.

grammars.title: Ty and vy — two kinds of "you", and the choice isn't about number
body: Slovak sorts the person you're talking to the way French and German do. What confuses beginners: *vy* has two jobs at once.

head: Form
Say it
Used with
Example
rows: one person, casual — friends, people your age, children, family
one person, polite — strangers, shop staff, lecturers, older people

after: **The verb form is the same for both jobs of *vy*.** So *Ako sa voláte?* can mean "What is your name?" (polite) or "What are your names?" — the situation tells you which. That saves you a whole table.

**A practical rule for beginners: when in doubt, use *vy*.** Using *vy* with a friend sounds a bit stiff and is instantly forgiven; using *ty* with an older stranger sounds rude. Slovaks usually offer to switch to *ty* first, with the sentence *Môžeme si tykať?* ("Can we say *ty* to each other?"). Answer *Áno, samozrejme!*
The greeting *ahoj* and the form *vy* never go together. The pairs are locked: **ahoj + ty**, **dobrý deň + vy**. If you remember one thing from this page, remember those pairs.

blocks.text: The ten phrases below aren't grammar to memorize — they're an emergency toolkit. Learn them whole now; understand how they're built later.

head: Slovenčina
Say it
English
rows: You're welcome; please; here you are
Ako sa to povie po slovensky?
AH-koh sah toh POH-vyeh poh SLOH-vehn-skee
How do you say that in Slovak?

blocks.text: *Prosím* is the most versatile word in Slovak. It means "please, go ahead" when offering a seat, "here you are" when handing something over, "hello?" when answering the phone, "yes?" when a waiter comes to your table, and "you're welcome" in reply to thanks. If you could learn only one word from this page, learn this one.

*Prepáčte* is the polite form; to a friend say *prepáč*. It covers two jobs — apologizing and getting someone's attention. To squeeze past in a crowd, Slovaks more often say *s dovolením* ("with permission").

Look at *po slovensky* and *po anglicky*. This *po …-sky* form is what you use for "in … (language)", not the name of the language. So: *po slovensky, po anglicky, po indonézsky, po nemecky*. It never changes form, so you can treat it as one fixed word.

sections.title: Greetings by time of day and politeness

blocks.text: Slovak sorts greetings along two axes at once: what time it is, and how close you are to the other person. This table covers both.

head: Slovenčina
Say it
When to use it
rows: Good day — all day, the safest polite greeting
Good night — only when parting for bed
Hi/bye — casual, sounds a little old-fashioned and warm

blocks.text: The one you'll need most is **dobrý deň**. It's polite, never wrong, and works from morning to evening. If you're unsure what time of day it is by Slovak standards, just use this.

One habit worth copying: in Slovakia, **entering a small space means greeting**. A lift, a doctor's waiting room, a train compartment, a small shop — people say *dobrý deň* to strangers, and silence actually feels rude. When you leave, say *dovidenia*.

blocks.title: Dobrý, dobré, dobrú — why does it keep changing?
items: It's not a typo. Slovak adjectives follow the gender of their noun: *deň* (day) masculine → *dobrý deň*; *ráno* (morning) neuter → *dobré ráno*; *noc* (night) feminine → *dobrú noc*.
For now, learn the four greetings as whole chunks. The rule is introduced gradually in unit 3 and completed in unit 18. But if you can already see the pattern, you're halfway there.
